verifiedClaims.claim: Maximum medical improvement is a medical determination — not a legal one — that a patient's condition has stabilized to the point where no further significant improvement is expected from continued medical treatment.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Regs. 67-506(B) ('the authorized health care provider reports the claimant has reached maximum medical improvement'); S.C. Code § 42-9-260(D)
verifiedClaims.note: The physician reports MMI; what follows from it (stopping benefits, rating) is decided by the Board or Commission when disputed. Accurate as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: MMI can be revised. If your condition unexpectedly worsens or a new treatment becomes available, the MMI determination can potentially be revisited, though the procedural rules for doing so differ between personal injury and workers' compensation contexts.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-104(a)(1), (b) (change in condition; application within two years of the last income-benefit payment, four years for § 34-9-263 benefits); S.C. Code § 42-17-90(A) (review for change of condition, not after twelve months from the last payment of compensation)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. If the refresh adds the deadlines: Georgia two years from the last income-benefit payment (§ 34-9-104(b)); South Carolina twelve months from the last payment of compensation (§ 42-17-90(A)).

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia: The employer or insurer has the right to select the authorized treating physician (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201). This physician's MMI determination is presumptively valid unless challenged.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia does not let the employer pick the doctor outright. The employer must post a Panel of Physicians of at least six physicians, at least one an orthopedic surgeon and no more than two industrial clinics; the employee 'may accept the services of a physician selected by the employer from the panel or may select another physician from the panel' and 'may make one change from one physician to another on the same panel without prior authorization of the board' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201(b)(1)). If the employer fails to post a valid panel, 'an employee may select any physician to render service at the expense of the employer' (§ 34-9-201(f)). No statute makes the treating physician's MMI opinion 'presumptively valid'; the Board weighs it against other medical evidence at a hearing.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201(b)(1), (c), (f); SBWC Board Rule 201; SBWC FAQ 'What do I do about a doctor?'
verifiedClaims.note: Replace with: 'Georgia: The employer posts a panel of at least six physicians and you choose your authorized treating physician from it; you may switch once within the panel without Board approval (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201). That physician's MMI opinion carries the most weight before the State Board unless you challenge it with other medical evidence.' Same correction as facts-1652.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina: The employer similarly directs initial medical care, though the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission may authorize a change of physician in certain circumstances (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 42-15-60(A) (employer furnishes 'an attending physician and any medical care or treatment that is considered necessary by the attending physician' which 'the employee shall accept, unless otherwise ordered by the commission for good cause shown'); SCWCC Injured Worker FAQs ('your employer has the right to choose your treating doctor'; if a second-opinion request is denied, 'you may request a hearing')
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. 'Similarly' now reads oddly once the Georgia bullet is corrected to the panel rule; change to 'In South Carolina the employer chooses the treating doctor outright'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia TTD: Paid at two-thirds of your average weekly wage, subject to a maximum weekly benefit set annually by the State Board of Workers' Compensation (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261). TTD benefits are available for up to 400 weeks.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two-thirds of the average weekly wage 'but not more than $800.00 per week nor less than $50.00 per week', 'for a maximum period of 400 weeks from the date of injury', except that a catastrophic injury under § 34-9-200.1(g) is paid 'until such time as the employee undergoes a change in condition for the better' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261). The $800 cap applies to injuries on or after July 1, 2023 (Ga. L. 2023, p. 416/HB 480) and is unchanged in the 2025 Code. The maximum is written into the statute by the General Assembly; the State Board does not set it annually.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261 (2025 Code); SBWC FAQ 'How much will my weekly benefits be?'
verifiedClaims.note: Replace 'subject to a maximum weekly benefit set annually by the State Board of Workers' Compensation' with 'capped by statute at $800 per week for injuries on or after July 1, 2023'. 400 weeks is correct; add 'except for catastrophic injuries'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina TTD: Paid at 66 2/3% of your average weekly wage, subject to a maximum set by the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). TTD benefits continue until you return to work or reach MMI.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 66 2/3% of the average weekly wage, but 'not more each week than the average weekly wage in this State for the preceding fiscal year' and never more than 500 weeks except lifetime cases (S.C. Code § 42-9-10(A), (C)). The cap is the state average weekly wage certified by the S.C. Department of Employment and Workforce and published by the Commission: $1,189.94 per week for injuries on or after January 1, 2026 ($1,134.43 for 2025 injuries). MMI does not end TTD by itself: within 150 days of notice the employer may stop payments only on the grounds in § 42-9-260(B) (return to work, full-duty release with a comparable job offered, light-duty release with light-duty work provided, etc.); once an employee 'has been declared as having reached maximum medical improvement, the employer may request a hearing to address the termination' (§ 42-9-260(D)), and after 150 days the employer 'shall continue payment of temporary compensation until the Commission finds the employer's representative may terminate compensation' (Reg. 67-506(B), Form 21).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 42-9-10; § 42-9-260(B), (D), (F); S.C. Code Regs. 67-505, 67-506; SCWCC Compensation Rates
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite the second sentence: 'TTD is capped at 500 weeks and normally ends when you return to work or are released to full duty; after MMI the insurer must ask the Commission for permission to stop it (S.C. Code § 42-9-260).' If a dollar figure is added it must carry its date-of-injury range.

verifiedClaims.claim: Once you reach MMI, if you have a permanent impairment, your benefits transition from temporary to permanent.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In Georgia PPD 'shall not become payable so long as the employee is entitled to benefits under Code Section 34-9-261 or 34-9-262' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(b)(2)); TTD is not ended by MMI but by return to work, a full-duty release, the 400-week cap, or the light-duty conversion rule — an employee released to restricted work is moved to TPD after 52 consecutive weeks and can draw no more than 78 aggregate weeks of TTD while capable of restricted work (§ 34-9-104(a)(2)). In South Carolina the transition after MMI requires Commission approval once 150 days have run (§ 42-9-260(D); Reg. 67-506(B)).
verifiedClaims.note: Change to 'Once you reach MMI and your temporary benefits end, if you have a permanent impairment your benefits shift from temporary to permanent — in Georgia PPD is not paid while TTD or TPD is owed (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263), and in South Carolina the insurer needs the Commission's permission to stop TTD after MMI (S.C. Code § 42-9-260).' Most consequential finding together with the 'MMI ends TTD' sentences in the Key Takeaways and FAQs.

verifiedClaims.claim: Permanent total disability (PTD): In rare cases involving catastrophic injuries, you may be found permanently and totally disabled, entitling you to benefits for the rest of your life.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: a catastrophic injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1(g)) is exempt from the 400-week cap and weekly benefits continue 'until such time as the employee undergoes a change in condition for the better' (§ 34-9-261); a rebuttable presumption that the injury is no longer catastrophic arises at Social Security full retirement age (§ 34-9-200.1(g)(6)(B)). South Carolina: total disability is capped at 500 weeks except that a paraplegic, a quadriplegic, or a person 'who has suffered physical brain damage' 'shall receive the benefits for life' (S.C. Code § 42-9-10(A), (C)); loss of two of hands, arms, shoulders, feet, legs, hips or eyes is total and permanent disability (§ 42-9-10(B)).
verifiedClaims.note: 'For the rest of your life' is literally true only for South Carolina's paraplegia, quadriplegia and brain-damage cases and for Georgia catastrophic cases while the disability lasts. Reword: 'entitling you to benefits beyond the ordinary caps — for life in South Carolina paraplegia, quadriplegia and brain-injury cases, and in Georgia for as long as the catastrophic disability continues.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Ongoing authorized treatment remains covered (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Ongoing authorized treatment remains covered, for a maximum of 400 weeks from the date of injury for non-catastrophic injuries on or after July 1, 2013; no time cap for catastrophic injuries or pre-July-2013 injuries (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200(a)(1)-(2)). Prosthetic, spinal-cord-stimulator and durable-medical-equipment maintenance is exempt from the 400 weeks if first furnished within them (§ 34-9-200(a)(3)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200(a); SBWC FAQ 'How long will I receive medical benefits?'
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell, and the same correction applies to the 'Post-MMI Medical Treatment (WC)' Georgia cell ('Authorized medical treatment continues to be covered after MMI'). Add '(up to 400 weeks for non-catastrophic injuries)'. Same finding as facts-1697.

verifiedClaims.claim: Ongoing authorized treatment remains covered (S.C. Code § 42-15-60)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Covered for ten weeks and 'for an additional time as in the judgment of the commission will tend to lessen the period of disability' (S.C. Code § 42-15-60(A)); lifetime only where total and permanent disability results (§ 42-15-60(C)). After a Form 16 permanent-disability agreement the employer owes no further treatment after one year from full payment unless the form says otherwise (§ 42-15-60(B)(1)); a lapse in authorized treatment of more than one year ends the obligation (§ 42-15-60(B)(3)); a clincher (Agreement and Final Release) ends medical benefits (Reg. 67-801(E)).
verifiedClaims.note: Table cell, and the same correction applies to the 'Post-MMI Medical Treatment (WC)' South Carolina cell. Change to 'Treatment the Commission finds will lessen disability remains covered; ends one year after a Form 16 settlement is paid out or after a one-year lapse in treatment (S.C. Code § 42-15-60)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: The transition from TTD to PPD often results in a significant reduction in weekly benefit payments.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In both states PPD is paid at the same two-thirds rate as TTD, subject to the same weekly maximum: Georgia PPD is 'two-thirds of the employee's average weekly wage' 'subject to the maximum and minimum limitations on weekly income benefits specified in Code Section 34-9-261' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(c)); South Carolina scheduled awards are 'sixty-six and two-thirds percent of the average weekly wages' and 'subject to the same limitations as to maximum and minimum as set out in Section 42-9-10' (S.C. Code § 42-9-30). What changes is the duration: PPD runs for the impairment percentage times the scheduled weeks, so total benefits are usually far smaller than continued TTD.
verifiedClaims.note: The weekly check does not shrink; the number of weeks does. Rewrite: 'The transition from TTD to PPD usually means a large reduction in total benefits: PPD is paid at the same weekly rate but only for a fixed number of weeks set by the impairment rating and the schedule.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Most physicians use the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment as the standard reference for calculating impairment ratings. The edition used matters — Georgia workers' compensation generally references the AMA Guides, and South Carolina does as well, though the specific edition and application may vary.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia fixes the edition by statute: 'any percentage of disability or bodily loss ratings shall be based upon Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, fifth edition, published by the American Medical Association' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(d)); the SBWC FAQ repeats 'fifth edition'. South Carolina's statute names no edition; Reg. 67-1101(B) lets the value of an unlisted organ or body part 'be determined in accordance with the American Medical Association's Guide to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, or any other accepted medical treatise or authority', and the Commission decides disability, not just impairment.
verifiedClaims.note: Replace 'Georgia workers' compensation generally references the AMA Guides ... may vary' with 'Georgia workers' compensation requires ratings under the fifth edition (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263); South Carolina's Commission accepts the AMA Guides or any other accepted medical authority and does not mandate an edition.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In workers' compensation: PPD benefits are calculated based on the impairment rating multiplied by the number of weeks assigned to the affected body part in the statutory schedule.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(c); S.C. Code § 42-9-30(20); SCWCC FAQ ('a percentage of loss of use of a single body part or a percentage of permanent disability to the whole person multiplied by a statutorily determined number of weeks and your average weekly wage')
verifiedClaims.note: Correct in both states.

verifiedClaims.claim: Obtain an independent evaluation from a physician of your choosing (at your own expense, though your attorney may advance the cost)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia pays for one. 'The employee, after an accepted compensable injury and within 120 days of receipt of any income benefits, shall have the right to one examination at a reasonable time and place, within this state or within 50 miles of the employee's residence, by a duly qualified physician or surgeon designated by the employee and to be paid for by the employer' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e)); the employee must give written notice within the 120 days (Board Rule 202(e)). It may not repeat diagnostic tests already done unless someone other than the employer pays any cost over $250.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e); SBWC Board Rule 202(e)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace with: 'Use your one-time independent medical examination by a physician of your choosing at the insurer's expense — the request must be made within 120 days of your first income-benefit check (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e)).' 'At your own expense' misstates a right the worker pays for by missing the window.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, MMI ends TTD and triggers PPD based on impairment rating (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No Georgia statute ends TTD at MMI. TTD runs up to 400 weeks until a return to work, a full-duty release, or the light-duty conversion rule (52 consecutive / 78 aggregate weeks capable of restricted work, § 34-9-104(a)(2)); PPD becomes payable only when the employee is no longer entitled to TTD or TPD (§ 34-9-263(b)(2)). MMI is when the rating is assigned, not when TTD stops.
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned; PPD (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD ends, and MMI alone does not end TTD.' Renders in the Key Takeaways box above the article.

verifiedClaims.claim: catastrophic injuries get lifetime benefits (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Catastrophic injuries are exempt from the 400-week cap and paid until a change in condition for the better (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261), with a rebuttable presumption at full retirement age that the injury is no longer catastrophic (§ 34-9-200.1(g)(6)(B)).
verifiedClaims.note: Change to 'catastrophic injuries are not subject to the 400-week caps (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, MMI triggers PPD within the 500-week cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10, § 42-9-30)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 42-9-10(A); § 42-9-30; S.C. Code Regs. 67-801(A) (settlement after MMI)
verifiedClaims.note: Acceptable shorthand; the 500-week limit and the schedule are correctly cited.

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical benefits continue after MMI in both states.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: up to 400 weeks from injury for non-catastrophic injuries on or after July 1, 2013 (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200(a)(2)). South Carolina: for as long as the Commission finds treatment will lessen disability; ends one year after a Form 16 settlement is paid or after a one-year lapse in treatment (S.C. Code § 42-15-60(A), (B)).
verifiedClaims.note: Add 'subject to Georgia's 400-week limit for non-catastrophic injuries'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your doctor assigns an impairment rating at MMI that quantifies any permanent loss of function.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(d); SBWC FAQ ('The authorized treating physician determines ratings'); SCWCC FAQ
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your treating physician makes the MMI determination. However, the workers' comp insurer or the opposing party's insurance company may request an Independent Medical Examination (IME) if they disagree.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(a) (employee 'if so requested by his or her employer, shall submit himself or herself to examination ... by a duly qualified physician or surgeon designated and paid by the employer or the board'); S.C. Code § 42-15-80(A)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct for workers' compensation in both states.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, reaching MMI typically ends temporary total disability (TTD) benefits and triggers a transition to permanent partial disability (PPD) benefits based on your impairment rating (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: MMI does not end TTD in Georgia. PPD 'shall not become payable so long as the employee is entitled to benefits under Code Section 34-9-261 or 34-9-262' (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263(b)(2)); TTD ends on return to work, full-duty release, the 400-week cap, or conversion to TPD after 52 consecutive weeks (78 aggregate) of being capable of restricted work (§ 34-9-104(a)(2)).
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned. It does not by itself end TTD — TTD continues until you return to work, are released to full duty, or hit the 400-week cap — and PPD (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD stops.' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: For catastrophic injuries, lifetime benefits may continue under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1. Medical benefits continue regardless of MMI.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Catastrophic benefits are not capped at 400 weeks and continue until a change in condition for the better (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261; definition § 34-9-200.1(g)). Medical benefits continue after MMI but, for non-catastrophic injuries on or after July 1, 2013, only for 400 weeks from the date of injury (§ 34-9-200(a)(2)).
verifiedClaims.note: Change to 'For catastrophic injuries the 400-week caps do not apply (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1). Medical benefits continue after MMI, for up to 400 weeks in non-catastrophic cases.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, MMI similarly ends TTD and triggers PPD benefits based on impairment rating and loss of earning capacity (S.C. Code § 42-9-30).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: After MMI the employer 'may request a hearing to address the termination of temporary disability payments' (S.C. Code § 42-9-260(D)); after 150 days from notice it 'shall continue payment of temporary compensation until the Commission finds the employer's representative may terminate compensation' (Reg. 67-506(B), Form 21). Scheduled PPD is under § 42-9-30; wage-loss (partial disability) benefits are under § 42-9-20.
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'In South Carolina, MMI lets the insurer ask the Commission to stop TTD (S.C. Code § 42-9-260) and starts the permanent-disability phase — scheduled PPD by impairment rating (§ 42-9-30) or wage-loss benefits (§ 42-9-20).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: The 500-week overall benefit cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10) continues to apply.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 42-9-10(A); § 42-9-30(22); S.C. Code Regs. 67-1101(C) ('The maximum period of compensation for a combination of injuries is the legislative criterion of five hundred weeks')
verifiedClaims.note: Correct, with the lifetime exception in § 42-9-10(C).

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical benefits for the work injury continue after MMI with no time limit.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: There are limits. The employer provides treatment for ten weeks plus 'an additional time as in the judgment of the commission will tend to lessen the period of disability' (S.C. Code § 42-15-60(A)); after a Form 16 permanent-disability agreement, no further treatment after one year from full payment unless the form provides otherwise (§ 42-15-60(B)(1)); no obligation after a lapse in authorized treatment of more than one year (§ 42-15-60(B)(3)); a change-of-condition claim must be brought within twelve months of the last payment of compensation (§ 42-17-90(A)); a clincher ends medical benefits (Reg. 67-801(E)). Lifetime medical is reserved for total and permanent disability (§ 42-15-60(C)).
verifiedClaims.note: Replace with: 'Medical benefits for the work injury can continue after MMI as long as the Commission finds treatment will lessen your disability — but they end one year after a Form 16 settlement is paid out or after a year without authorized treatment, so keep treating (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Settling before MMI means you do not know the full extent of your injuries or future medical costs. You risk accepting far less than your claim is worth. The exception is catastrophic injuries with obvious permanent disability and low insurance policy limits, where early settlement may make strategic sense.
verifiedClaims.note: Strategy advice, no legal fact to verify; consistent with S.C. Code Regs. 67-801(A) (WC settlements follow MMI).

verifiedClaims.claim: (2) have your attorney challenge the determination through the workers' comp board or in court
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In a workers' compensation claim the challenge is a hearing request — Form WC-14 with the Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation, Form 50 with the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission (or Section III of the Form 15 if payments were stopped, § 42-9-260(C)). A personal-injury MMI dispute is not litigated 'in court' as such; it is a battle of medical experts at trial.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SBWC FAQ (Form WC-14); S.C. Code Regs. 67-207; S.C. Code § 42-9-260(C)
verifiedClaims.note: Change to '(2) have your attorney request a hearing — Form WC-14 with Georgia's State Board or Form 50 with South Carolina's Commission'. Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: (4) request that the court appoint an independent medical examiner
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e) (employee's own one-time examination at employer expense within 120 days of income benefits); § 34-9-202(a) (examination by a physician 'designated and paid by the employer or the board'); S.C. Code § 42-15-80(A) (examination 'ordered by the commission'); S.C. Code Regs. 67-602(C)
verifiedClaims.note: No court-appointed IME procedure exists in either state's workers' compensation or personal-injury practice. Replace item (4) with: 'in Georgia, use your one-time independent examination at the insurer's expense within 120 days of your first income-benefit check (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e)); in South Carolina, ask the Commission to order an examination (S.C. Code § 42-15-80).'

statuteCitations.name: Change in condition — definition; 52-consecutive / 78-aggregate-week conversion of TTD to TPD for non-catastrophic employees released to restricted work; two-year window to reopen income benefits
Medical care — reasonably required treatment; 400-week maximum for non-catastrophic injuries on or after July 1, 2013; Board may order a change of physician (subsection (b))
Panel of Physicians — at least six physicians, one orthopedic; employee selects from the panel and may change once without Board approval; any physician at employer expense if no panel is posted
Examinations — employer-requested examinations; subsection (e) employee's one-time examination by a physician of their choice at employer expense within 120 days of receipt of income benefits
Temporary total disability — two-thirds of AWW, $800/week maximum for injuries on or after July 1, 2023, 400 weeks; catastrophic injuries exempt from the cap
Temporary partial disability — two-thirds of the wage difference, $533/week maximum, 350 weeks
Permanent partial disability — schedule (body as a whole 300 weeks, arm/leg 225); not payable while TTD or TPD is owed; ratings under the AMA Guides, fifth edition
Personal injury statute of limitations — two years
Apportionment — plaintiff 50 percent or more responsible recovers nothing
Total disability — 66 2/3% of AWW up to the state average weekly wage; 500-week maximum; lifetime for paraplegia, quadriplegia, physical brain damage
Partial disability — 66 2/3% of the wage difference, 340 weeks (the section the post miscites as § 42-9-15)
Scheduled losses — weeks per member; partial loss in proportion; unlisted parts up to 500 weeks
Starting, suspending and terminating temporary compensation — 150-day rule; employer hearing request after MMI (subsection (D)); Commission approval required after 150 days

Medical treatment — employer furnishes the attending physician; ten weeks plus such time as the Commission judges will lessen disability; one-year limits after a Form 16 settlement or a lapse in treatment; lifetime in total-permanent cases
Examinations — employee submits to examination requested by the employer or ordered by the Commission; may have own physician present at own expense
Change of condition — review within twelve months of the last payment of compensation
Personal injury statute of limitations — three years
